prompt: This is the cancellation activity diagram with its words removed. Put each name on the part it belongs to.
hint: Two thick bars: the first splits the flow, the second waits.

prompt: In the cancellation diagram, what does the join before the confirmation guarantee?
hint: A join waits for every flow that the fork started.

choices.text: That the refund happens before the seat is released
choices.why: The fork lets the two run in either order; the join only waits for both to finish.

choices.text: Nobody is told until both are done
choices.why: Right: the passenger is never told refunded while the money has not been asked for.

choices.text: That one of the two flows finishing is enough
choices.why: That would be a merge; a join waits for all its incoming flows.

choices.text: That the payment gateway approves the refund
choices.why: The diagram says the refund was requested and carried out, not that it can be refused.

prompt: Drawing the cancellation policy as a diagram found a gap in Otávio's paragraph. What was it?
hint: The decision needed one more guard.

choices.text: The fee for changing a ticket was missing
choices.why: The paragraph stated the fee; the gap was a case with no rule.

choices.text: Refunds were sent to the wrong account
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the diagram found a missing case, not a wrong one.

choices.text: A trip that has already left
choices.why: Yes: the paragraph said before departure twice and never said what happens after it.

choices.text: The station agent's lane was missing
choices.why: Agents do not take part in an online cancellation; three lanes were enough.

prompt: Match each BPMN element to its activity-diagram equivalent.
hint: X chooses; + runs in parallel.

prompt: In BPMN, Carcará's process needs something from the payment company. How is that drawn?
hint: One organisation cannot tell another what to do next.

choices.text: A sequence flow from Carcará's task into the other pool
choices.why: Sequence flows stay inside one pool; between pools only messages pass.

choices.text: As a dashed message flow between the two pools
choices.why: Right: the pool boundary is where our process ends and their system begins.

choices.text: As a lane for the payment company inside Carcará's pool
choices.why: A lane is part of the same organisation's process; the payment company runs its own.

choices.text: A parallel gateway
choices.why: Gateways split or join flows inside a process; they do not cross organisations.

prompt: Celeste needs a five-step procedure for station staff when the system is down. Which notation does the lesson suggest?
hint: Short, few decisions, a non-technical reader.

choices.text: BPMN, because it is a standard
choices.why: BPMN pays off when a process crosses organisations or a tool runs it; here it is more than the reader needs.

choices.text: A UML activity diagram with partitions
choices.why: Possible, and still more notation than a short procedure for this reader needs.

choices.text: A flowchart
choices.why: Yes: the one process notation a non-technical reader follows without a legend.

choices.text: A state machine of the station
choices.why: A procedure is a sequence of steps; a state machine follows one object's conditions.

prompt: This is the ticket's state machine with its words removed. Put each name on the part it belongs to.
hint: One arrow leaves a state and comes back to it.

prompt: A draft state machine for a ticket has the states Held, Validating payment, Sending e-mail and Paid. What is wrong?
hint: Could you find a ticket in that state tomorrow morning?

choices.text: It has too few states
choices.why: The count is not the problem; two of the four are not states at all.

choices.text: Two of them are steps that last milliseconds, not conditions
choices.why: Right: they are things the system does, so they belong in an activity diagram or inside a transition.

choices.text: State names should be verbs
choices.why: The opposite: states are adjectives or past participles; verbs name steps.

choices.text: Paid should be a final state
choices.why: A paid ticket can still be boarded, refunded or become a no-show.

prompt: A transition label is written event [___] / action: the part in brackets is a condition that must be true.
hint: The same word names the conditions on an activity diagram's branches.

prompt: Why must the boarding app's offline list contain only tickets in Paid?
hint: What would an Expired ticket on the list allow?

choices.text: Boarding an unpaid passenger
choices.why: Yes: everything that checks a ticket has to agree with the state machine.

choices.text: Because the list would be too large for the phone otherwise
choices.why: Size is not the reason the lesson gives; correctness is.

choices.text: Because Held tickets have no seat number
choices.why: A held ticket has a seat; it has not been paid for.

choices.text: Because Refunded tickets are unreadable at the door
choices.why: They can be scanned and must be refused; that is exactly why they stay off the list.

prompt: A state table for six states and six events has how many cells to decide?
hint: States times events.

prompt: What does a blank cell in a state table mean?
hint: Every cell has to be filled.

choices.text: The event is impossible in that state
choices.why: It may be very possible: the late payment was a blank cell that happened on a Friday before São João.

choices.text: A question the design has not answered
choices.why: Right: whatever the code then does is an accident rather than a decision.

choices.text: The transition should be ignored
choices.why: Ignore is a valid answer, and it has to be written in the cell to be a decision.

choices.text: A final state
choices.why: Final states are drawn as such; a blank cell is a missing decision in any row.

prompt: A payment approval arrives for a ticket that has already expired and whose seat was resold. What did Carcará decide?
hint: The seat is gone; the money is not.

choices.text: Mark the ticket paid and move the other passenger
choices.why: That is what the code did before anybody decided, and it put two passengers on one seat.

choices.text: Ignore the approval; the gateway will cancel it on its own
choices.why: The passenger would have paid for nothing, with nobody telling them.

choices.text: Refund it, keep it Expired and offer the nearest seats
choices.why: Yes: written into the table, then onto the diagram, into a test and into a decision record.

choices.text: Hold the payment until a seat frees up
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson's decision keeps the money waiting; it is refunded automatically.

prompt: The gateway sends the same payment approved webhook twice for a Paid ticket. What should the cell say?
hint: Retries are normal.

choices.text: Raise an error so somebody investigates
choices.why: A retried webhook is the normal case, not an incident.

choices.text: Record a second payment
choices.why: That is the double count idempotency exists to prevent.

choices.text: Move the ticket to Boarded
choices.why: Only a scan at the door boards a ticket.

choices.text: Ignore it
choices.why: Right: the same event twice changes nothing.

prompt: Carcará calls the payment gateway, yet the gateway is upstream. Why?
hint: Upstream is about whose model wins.

choices.text: Because the gateway sends webhooks to Carcará
choices.why: The lesson says a webhook does not change the direction; who opens the connection is not the point.

choices.text: Its model decides and Carcará adapts
choices.why: Yes: changes flow from U to D, whatever the calls do.

choices.text: Because external systems are drawn on top
choices.why: Position on the page says nothing about upstream; the U and D do.

choices.text: Because Carcará pays the gateway
choices.why: Money flows one way and models another; the relationship is about models.

prompt: Match each abbreviation on a context map to its meaning.
hint: Two sit at the upstream end, two at the downstream end.

pairs.right: one documented protocol for every client
the downstream translates the upstream's model
the downstream takes the upstream's model as it is

right_distractors: the two teams share a database

prompt: Why does changing the published language between Sales and Boarding need a migration plan?
hint: Where is that format stored?

choices.text: The drivers' 300 phones store it offline
choices.why: Right: old phones still running the old format have to keep working, so the format got a version number.

choices.text: Because Boarding uses an anticorruption layer
choices.why: The map says Boarding is conformist, which is why it is so exposed to the change.

choices.text: Because the format is defined by Frota
choices.why: Sales publishes it; Frota is upstream of Sales, not of Boarding.

choices.text: Because published languages are forbidden from changing
choices.why: They can change, carefully, with versions; that is the plan.

prompt: Before the map, Frota's model leaked into eleven classes of Sales. What did naming the anticorruption layer change?
hint: Where does the translation live now?

choices.text: Frota was replaced with a new system
choices.why: Frota will not change; the layer exists because of that.

choices.text: Sales became conformist to Frota
choices.why: That would have spread Frota's model further, not contained it.

choices.text: Frota's team started planning for Sales
choices.why: That would be customer and supplier, and the lesson says Frota will not change.

choices.text: The translation moved into one place
choices.why: Yes: the next Frota upgrade broke one class instead of eleven.

prompt: Match the names in a diagram's boxes to the picture they give away.
hint: Verbs, adjectives, areas, running things.

prompt: A state machine reads Held → Validating payment → Paid. What are the two ways the lesson gives to fix it?
hint: Either it is a real condition, or it is not a state at all.

choices.text: Rename it Awaiting confirmation with its own transitions, or fold it into the transition
choices.why: Right: either the ticket really waits there, or validating is a step inside the arrow.

choices.text: Turn the diagram into a sequence diagram
choices.why: The question is about the ticket's states; a sequence diagram answers a different one.

choices.text: Add a guard
choices.why: A guard conditions a transition; it does not decide whether a box is a state.

choices.text: Make Validating payment the initial pseudostate
choices.why: The initial pseudostate is not a state the ticket stays in.
